definition: A metamaterial is an engineered material whose internal shape can be designed to influence mechanical, acoustic, or other behavior.
context: Matter uses repeating cells to show how architecture can change a material concept.

definition: Geometry, or material architecture, is the arrangement of shapes and spaces that makes up a structure.
context: Changing the cell geometry is the main design action in the studio.

definition: A lattice is a connected framework of repeated small units with solid parts and open spaces.
context: The studio renders lattices as repeated cells inside midsoles, cores, and liners.

definition: A unit cell is the smallest repeatable piece used to build a larger periodic structure.
context: Structure view isolates the pattern that repeats across the 3D model.

definition: A periodic structure repeats the same unit cell at regular intervals.
context: The Repetition control changes how many cells appear along X, Y, and Z.

definition: Cell size is the overall dimension of one repeating lattice cell.
context: Matter lets you set an illustrative cell size in millimetres.

definition: A strut is a slender solid member that links points in a framework, and its diameter is its width.
context: Octet and Kelvin models use struts to make their open networks visible.

definition: Wall thickness is the distance through a sheet-like solid surface.
context: For the sheet gyroid, the Thickness control changes wall thickness rather than a strut diameter.

definition: Density is mass per unit volume, while relative density is the fraction of a lattice volume occupied by solid material.
context: The property card shows a rough illustrative estimate; it does not calculate the actual solid volume of the 3D mesh.

definition: A load path is the route through which an applied force travels through a structure.
context: The octet lesson asks you to inspect the triangular paths inside the wing core.

definition: Deformation is a change in an object’s shape or size caused by forces or motion.
context: Behavior mode shows schematic deformation for learning, not a calculated result.

definition: Stiffness describes how strongly an object resists being deformed by a load.
context: The app uses “light but stiff” as a qualitative label for the octet truss.

definition: Modulus is a number that describes a material’s elastic resistance to being stretched or compressed.
context: The property card presents an illustrative modulus range in MPa.

definition: A megapascal is one million pascals, a unit commonly used for stress and modulus.
context: Matter labels material modulus values and bounds in MPa.

definition: Voigt and Reuss bounds are ideal mixture estimates based on equal strain and equal stress assumptions, respectively.
context: Matter reports both bounds for an ideal solid mixture and uses neither as a lattice-performance result.

definition: A two-phase mixture combines two different materials in specified proportions.
context: The secondary-material slider makes an ideal blend and does not assess manufacturability.

definition: TPU is a thermoplastic polyurethane that can behave like a flexible, rubber-like solid.
context: TPU elastomer is one of Matter’s illustrative base-material choices.

definition: PA12 is a nylon polymer known as polyamide 12.
context: Nylon PA12 is available as a contrasting illustrative base material.

definition: Aluminium and titanium are metals included as higher-modulus illustrative base-material choices.
context: Selecting either metal changes the app’s ideal solid-mixture inputs, not a validated lattice result.

definition: A gyroid is a continuously curved, repeating geometry that divides space into intertwined passages.
context: Matter places a gyroid-inspired network in the shoe midsole study.

definition: A sheet gyroid makes the gyroid pattern from continuous curved walls.
context: The Sheet gyroid variant lets you inspect curved walls through the open midsole.

definition: A skeletal gyroid represents the gyroid pattern as connected solid branches instead of a continuous sheet.
context: Matter contrasts the branch-like voids with the sheet-gyroid version.

definition: A minimal surface is a surface that locally minimizes area and has zero average curvature at each point.
context: The field guide identifies the gyroid as a mathematical minimal-surface geometry.

definition: An octet truss is a repeating framework built from tetrahedra (four triangular faces) and octahedra (eight triangular faces).
context: Matter uses an octet core in its aircraft-wing cutaway study.

definition: An anisotropic structure responds differently in different directions, while an isotropic one responds the same in every direction.
context: The Anisotropic octet stretches cells to make a preferred geometric direction visible.

definition: A graded structure changes a feature from place to place, while a uniform structure keeps that feature the same throughout the shown region.
context: Graded variants change wall, strut, or resonator dimensions across the study object.

definition: A re-entrant cell has ribs that point inward, creating an indented geometry.
context: Matter shows these inward ribs in the wearable knee-protection insert.

definition: An auxetic structure can become wider when it is pulled longer in a chosen direction.
context: The re-entrant lesson uses rib rotation to explain this idealized response.

definition: Poisson ratio is the negative of sideways strain divided by lengthwise strain: a negative value means a structure gets wider as it gets longer.
context: A negative value is the geometric idea behind Matter’s auxetic re-entrant cell.

definition: A Kelvin cell is a space-filling cell based on a truncated octahedron.
context: Matter curves a patch of Kelvin cells beneath a cycling-helmet shell.

definition: A truncated octahedron is a 14-faced solid with eight hexagonal faces and six square faces.
context: Its edge network is the geometric basis for the Kelvin-cell liner study.

definition: A honeycomb is a cellular structure made from repeating wall-enclosed cells, often hexagons.
context: Matter places honeycomb walls between the skins of a skateboard deck.

definition: A hexagonal cell is a six-sided cell shape.
context: The Honeycomb variants compare regular and elongated hexagonal cells.

definition: A local resonator is an internal part that can oscillate relative to the surrounding structure.
context: Matter animates internal masses inside a motor isolation mount to explain the idea.

definition: Resonance occurs when a system responds strongly near one of its natural frequencies.
context: The local-resonator guide describes wave effects near resonance without quantifying a mount.

definition: A mass–spring oscillator is a simple model in which a mass moves back and forth against a restoring spring force.
context: Matter uses this model to introduce the motion of a local resonator.

definition: Elastodynamic describes elastic waves and vibrations moving through a solid over time.
context: The Research Explorer filters a separate dataset of 2D elastodynamic designs.

definition: A band gap is a frequency interval in which waves cannot propagate in the dataset’s ideal infinite periodic model; its center is the midpoint and its width is the interval’s span.
context: The dataset controls search for records by their reported band-gap location and span.

definition: Frequency is the number of repeated cycles of a vibration or wave that occur each second.
context: Research Explorer expresses band-gap center and width in hertz.

definition: Wave propagation is the movement of a wave through a material or structure.
context: The band-gap note describes conditions where waves cannot propagate through an ideal model.

definition: A simulated design is evaluated with a computational model rather than directly measured on a physical specimen.
context: The UCI rows in Research Explorer are labeled simulated and remain separate from the 3D catalog.

definition: An evidence label states whether a record is measured, simulated, or illustrative.
context: Imported records must retain one of these labels alongside their source URL.

definition: A 15-bit source encoding is a string of 15 zeros and ones used by the dataset to represent a design record.
context: Matter displays the dataset code but says it is not a spatial reconstruction of a unit cell.

definition: The midsole is the shoe layer between the upper and outsole that commonly provides cushioning and structure.
context: Matter places the gyroid lattice in the midsole of its athletic-shoe anatomy study.

definition: The outsole is the bottom shoe layer that contacts the ground and can provide grip.
context: Matter labels the lowermost shoe part as the rubber outsole plus traction.

definition: An insole or sockliner is the layer inside a shoe that sits directly below the foot.
context: The shoe cutaway separates this foot-support layer above the midsole.

definition: A Strobel board is a thin shoe construction layer that forms a base for the upper and sits above the midsole.
context: Matter labels it as a structural layer in the exploded shoe view.

definition: The shoe upper is the part surrounding the foot, with components such as the tongue, laces, collar, and heel counter helping fit and hold it in place.
context: Matter groups the upper, tongue, and laces in one label and shows the collar and heel counter separately.

definition: An airfoil is a wing cross-section shaped to guide airflow and generate aerodynamic forces.
context: Matter keeps the wing’s outer airfoil shape while revealing its internal octet core.

definition: Wing skin is the thin outer aerodynamic covering, while a core is the internal layer held between outer skins in a lightweight built-up structure.
context: The cutaway moves an inspection skin aside to expose the core beneath it.

definition: A core is the internal layer between outer skins in a lightweight built-up structure.
context: Matter’s octet core sits inside the aircraft-wing cutaway.

definition: A cutaway is a view made by removing or moving part of an outer surface to reveal the inside.
context: The Cutaway button exposes lattice geometry inside application models.

definition: A helmet shell is the outer covering, a liner is the layer beneath it, and vents are openings through the shell.
context: Matter shows a Kelvin-cell liner beneath a vented helmet shell as an illustrative design study.

definition: A knee pad can combine an outer shell with an inner insert that follows the joint area.
context: Matter uses the re-entrant insert to illustrate geometric conformity around a flexed knee.

definition: A motor isolation mount is a support placed between a motor and its surroundings to manage transmitted vibration.
context: Matter animates a motor above local resonators without claiming a calculated vibration reduction.

definition: Uniform means the chosen feature stays the same throughout the structure.
context: A uniform lattice uses the same cell dimensions and member thickness throughout.

definition: Isotropic means a property is the same in every direction.
context: This contrasts with an anisotropic design, whose response depends on direction.

definition: The patella is your kneecap; a support ring surrounds it with a cushioned opening.
context: The knee study places a contoured ring in front of the fitted textile sleeve.

definition: A compression sleeve is a close-fitting stretch fabric that wraps around a limb.
context: The brace sleeve follows the thigh and lower leg while the joint bends.

definition: A tension dial tightens a cable, while side stays are reinforcing strips along the sides of a brace.
context: The knee model shows a laced dial and side supports that pivot at the knee.

definition: A headform is a shaped model of a human head used to inspect fit or perform controlled tests.
context: The helmet is fitted around a rigid mannequin head; it is not a biological injury simulation.

definition: A retention system holds protective equipment in place using straps, buckles or fitted bands.
context: The helmet straps join below each ear and pass under the chin.

definition: Gravity is the attraction that accelerates a released object downward.
context: The ball follows a parabolic path under constant gravity, shown in slow motion.

definition: A rebound is the upward motion after a collision; a less elastic collision gives a smaller rebound.
context: The illustrative ball loses speed at each contact and eventually rests on the shell.

definition: Tail stabilizers are the small rear aerodynamic surfaces that help control an aircraft’s orientation.
context: The horizontal tail and vertical fin sweep backward, away from the nose.

definition: A stiff object needs more force to bend or stretch by the same amount.
context: The octet truss uses triangles to resist deformation with relatively little solid material.

definition: Vibration is repeated back-and-forth motion around a resting position.
context: A local resonator uses an internal moving mass to influence particular vibration frequencies.

definition: A tetrahedron has four triangular faces; an octahedron has eight.
context: Their edges form the repeating triangulated framework in the octet truss.

definition: A load is a force acting on a material or structure.
context: A runner’s weight loads the sole, while an impact briefly loads the helmet liner.

definition: Tension is a pulling force; strain describes how much a dimension changes compared with its starting size.
context: Pulling a re-entrant lattice rotates its inward ribs and can make it widen.

definition: An airframe is the load-carrying structure of an aircraft, including its fuselage, wings and tail.
context: The wing cutaway shows one possible internal core within that structure.

definition: An aircraft engine provides thrust to move the aircraft through the air.
context: The engine hangs beneath the wing, which must carry the engine and aerodynamic loads.

definition: Grip tape is the rough surface under a skateboard rider’s feet; the deck skin is a structural outer layer below it.
context: Exploding the deck separates this upper layer from the honeycomb core.

definition: Trucks are the metal assemblies that attach the wheels to a skateboard; axles are the shafts the wheels turn around.
context: The truck assemblies connect the lightweight deck to the four wheels.

definition: Urethane is a polymer commonly used to make resilient skateboard wheels.
context: The wheels rotate as a visual demonstration; grip and rolling resistance are not calculated.

definition: A motor converts energy into rotation and can also produce unwanted vibration.
context: The local-resonator study shows a rotating motor mounted above an internal mass-and-spring network.

definition: A mounting skid is a base frame that holds equipment in position.
context: The skid stays anchored while the motor and internal resonator masses move.
